first.rationale: Onboarding completion and activation are both declining, and prior evidence indicates that shortening onboarding and reducing signup friction durably improved self-serve activation and time-to-value. Promotional pricing directly addresses the competitor threat but has documented 30-day retention harm, which conflicts with the sustainable qualified-revenue objective. Verify the two onboarding records before committing to calibrate the highest-leverage simplification test.

mid.rationale: Run a standard experiment shortening the self-serve onboarding flow, prioritizing removal or deferral of nonessential steps after signup. The verified onboarding result improved completion by 13%, reduced time-to-value by 2.1 days, and increased 30-day retention by 3%, directly addressing both current declines with evidence of durable value. Do not use promotional pricing despite competitive pressure: its documented retention harm conflicts with the long-term qualified-revenue objective. Keep signup-field reduction separate from this cycle because its SMB result included a 1% retention decline and was not replicated beyond SMB.

final2.rationale: Keep the committed onboarding-simplification experiment. It directly addresses the concurrent 4% completion and 6% activation declines and has verified evidence of higher completion (+13%), faster time-to-value (-2.1 days), and improved 30-day retention (+3%). The deeper competitor cut and increased SMB churn conversations heighten the commercial risk, but they do not establish that promotional pricing will prevent churn. Prior pricing evidence showed acquisition and revenue lift in price-sensitive SMBs alongside material 30-day retention harm, which conflicts with sustainable long-term qualified revenue. Monitor SMB churn pressure closely and revisit a tightly targeted retention intervention next cycle rather than displacing the only experiment with a known downstream-value risk.
